newsitem.title: USA: U.S. independent producers fear royalty proposal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. independent producers fear royalty proposal.

text.p: U.S. independent oil producers are nervous about proposed changes in the way the U.S. government calculates royalties for oil produced on federal lands, an industry official said Tuesday.
"We always thought it was more of a concern for big producers," said the official, who asked not to be named.

The Minerals Management Service proposed last month to tie oil royalty calculations to crude oil futures prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange, instead of basing royalties on oil companies' posted prices.
"It's a radical change," said the industry official.
The administration is eager to change the way it collects royalties because it believes posted prices do not reflect the true value of the oil being produced on federal land.
Independents plan to propose a different formula for collecting royalties, said Lew Ward, chairman of the Independent Petroleum Association of America.
"We want to make sure we pay on what we actually receive at the wellhead," Ward said at a news conference.
Smaller producers sell their oil to refiners or to oil gatherers for posted prices, which are generally lower than futures prices.
As a result, if MMS goes ahead with its proposed change, independents might end up paying royalties based on a market price that is higher than they receive for their oil.
Independents were caught off-guard by the MMS proposal even though the agency had floated the idea more than a year ago, an industry official said.

They first thought only big oil companies would be affected, because the agency originally planned to use futures prices in its royalty formula only for producers who sold most of their oil in swaps or other transactions that did not involve arm's length exchanges of money.
Unlike big oil companies, most independents sell their oil in arm's length deals.
But the latest proposal from MMS expanded the potential universe of producers who would have to pay royalties based on futures prices.

Independents hope the agency will go slow in making any changes in its royalty collection. The agency has already extended the comment period and has postponed planned public meetings on the proposal by more than one month to give industry more time to evaluate it.
